reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: A malignant vascular tumour of intermediate to low-grade behaviour that can arise in soft tissue, bone, liver, lung and other organs
Frequently multifocal within an organ or presents synchronously in several sites, which can be mistaken for metastatic carcinoma
Defined in most cases by a WWTR1-CAMTA1 gene fusion, with a smaller subset carrying a YAP1-TFE3 fusion
CAMTA1 nuclear immunohistochemistry serves as a useful surrogate marker for the characteristic fusion
Histology shows cords and nests of epithelioid endothelial cells in a distinctive myxohyaline or chondroid stroma, with intracytoplasmic vacuoles representing primitive lumina
The cells express endothelial markers such as CD31, ERG and CD34, confirming vascular differentiation
Behaviour ranges from indolent to aggressive, and management spans surveillance, resection and systemic therapy depending on burden and risk features
reference.pathophysiology: Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is a malignant tumour of endothelial (vascular) origin defined in the great majority of cases by a WWTR1-CAMTA1 gene fusion, with a minority driven by a YAP1-TFE3 fusion. The fusion dysregulates the Hippo signalling pathway, leading to constitutive activation of transcriptional coactivators that promote endothelial cell proliferation. Tumour cells are epithelioid and grow as cords and small nests set in a characteristic myxohyaline stroma, and individual cells often contain intracytoplasmic vacuoles that represent attempts at forming primitive vascular lumina. Its multifocal presentation reflects the disease biology rather than metastatic spread from a single primary.
additionalDifferentials: Sclerosing or metastatic carcinoma of the liver or lung
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging of the affected organ and staging to map multifocal disease
Biopsy with histological assessment of epithelioid cords in myxohyaline stroma
Endothelial immunohistochemistry with CD31, ERG and CD34
CAMTA1 nuclear staining as a surrogate for the WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion
Molecular confirmation of WWTR1-CAMTA1 or YAP1-TFE3 fusion in ambiguous cases
redFlags: Large tumour size or high mitotic activity indicating more aggressive behaviour
Widespread multiorgan involvement or rapid progression
Pleural effusion, haemoptysis or significant pain suggesting aggressive disease
Features overlapping with epithelioid angiosarcoma, which is more aggressive
reference.prognosis: Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma has variable behaviour, and many cases follow an indolent course while others progress and metastasise, particularly those with larger size and higher mitotic activity. Risk stratification using size and mitotic count helps predict outcome and guide the intensity of treatment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing multifocal disease as metastatic carcinoma
Confusing it with the more aggressive epithelioid angiosarcoma
Overlooking vascular differentiation without endothelial immunostains
Assuming a uniformly indolent course without assessing risk features
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Wide surgical excision with negative margins for localised soft-tissue or bone disease as the primary curative approach
Watchful waiting with interval imaging for asymptomatic, indolent multifocal disease, since multifocality reflects disease biology rather than resectable metastasis
Systemic antiangiogenic therapy for progressive or symptomatic disease, using agents such as mTOR inhibitors, interferon-alpha, bevacizumab or pazopanib
Radiotherapy for unresectable or symptomatic osseous lesions and for local control after marginal resection
Orthopaedic stabilisation or reconstruction for structurally compromised weight-bearing bone
Risk stratification by tumour size and mitotic activity to determine the intensity of treatment and follow-up
Long-term surveillance imaging for local recurrence and new multifocal sites
Referral to a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team for coordinated care
